explanation: Brazil runs from about 5° N to about 34° S, the only country both lines cross. The Equator crosses Ecuador and Indonesia, and the Tropic crosses Australia.

claims.text: Both the Equator and the Tropic of Capricorn cross Brazil.
The Equator crosses Ecuador and Indonesia but the Tropic of Capricorn does not, and the Tropic of Capricorn crosses Australia but the Equator does not.
Brazil's territory runs from about 5° N to about 34° S.
Brazil is the only country crossed by both the Equator and the Tropic of Capricorn.

writerNotes: Self-check (§9.3). Lint: content:check reports no errors or warnings for this item. Claims: every checkable statement is listed; c3 carries numbers and c4 says 'only', so both are high; c1 and c2 are standard. Datasets: natural-earth ne_110m_admin_0_countries, latitude extents from the geometry: Brazil 5.24° N to 33.77° S (c3). Countries spanning 0°: Indonesia, DR Congo, Somalia, Kenya, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Congo, Gabon, Uganda. Countries spanning 23.44° S: Argentina, Chile, South Africa, Brazil, Botswana, Namibia, Mozambique, Madagascar, Australia, Paraguay. Brazil is the only name on both lists (c4). Australia's extent is 10.67° S to 43.63° S and Indonesia's 5.48° N to 10.36° S (c2). Rival test: Ecuador is the tempting name, since it is named after the Equator; Australia and Indonesia are each crossed by one of the two lines, so all three distractors are half right, which is what makes them tempting. Against the key: none. Volatility: evergreen, settled geography with no review date; no time words, and nothing depends on knowledge newer than mid-2026. Regional: uses only world-map knowledge. Style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens only, straight quotes, explanation of 27 words. Myths: every claim screened against content/reference/myths.json; no match. Mystery and encore: nothing of either kind to check in a practice item. Doubts: the 110m file leaves out small island states (Kiribati, São Tomé and Príncipe, Maldives), all far north of the Tropic of Capricorn, so c4 still holds; a bounding box can overstate a crossing, but Brazil's land is continuous across both lines.
